content.text: Every request passes through your middleware in the order of the

, and the response passes back in reverse. A middleware sees only what earlier middleware produced, guards only what comes after it, and can end the request early. Put one in the wrong place and the app still compiles and starts, but authentication, error handling or logging quietly does the wrong thing.

An API adds a small middleware that records who called which endpoint, for a compliance report. In production, every row says "anonymous", including calls made with valid tokens that the API accepted and answered. The middleware's code is fine. It's registered one line above
, so when it runs, nobody has read the token yet.
is a list of features to switch on. As long as every middleware is registered, the order of the
calls doesn't matter; the framework works out when each one should run.
Several things make that feel true. The order of
lines can go almost anywhere in the file and still work. If you don't call

calls aren't settings. Each one adds a step to a chain, and the chain runs in exactly the order you wrote.
The pipeline is a chain of nested calls
delegate that stands for everything registered after it. Code before
runs on the way in; code after it runs on the way out, once the rest of the pipeline has finished. So the first middleware you register sees the request first and the response last:
prints "A: request in", "B: request in", then "B: response out" and "A: response out". The endpoint runs in the middle, even though
comes first in the file: endpoints added to
always execute at the end of the pipeline.
A middleware sees only what ran before it
Middleware hands information down the chain through the
. Routing picks the endpoint, so the selected endpoint is always null before routing runs. Authentication reads the token or cookie and sets
, so anything that runs earlier sees an anonymous user. That's the audit bug: the middleware asked for the user before anyone had looked.
A middleware guards only what comes after it

The exception handler catches exceptions thrown by middleware registered after it, which is why the docs put it first. Register it below a middleware that throws, and the exception never reaches it: in production, the server answers with a bare 500 and no body instead of your error response. Authorization can stop a request before it reaches the endpoint, but any middleware registered before authorization has already run for that request. Place a check too late, and the work it was meant to prevent has already happened.
Some middleware ends the request early
A middleware that answers without calling
the pipeline: static files return a file, authorization returns a 401 or 403. Nothing registered after it runs for that request, while everything registered before it still runs its code after

written after it never runs at all.
